I have the honor to invite Ms. Bjorg Sankar, Assistant Secretary General for Policy Coordination in the Department of Economic and Social Affairs to make a statement.

Thank you very much, Chair. Good morning, Excellencies, Co-Chairs of the Committee. of experts of global geospatial information management, DGIM, distinguished delegates, observers, representatives of the global geospatial information community. And I would like to also say, dear colleagues, it gives me great pleasure this morning to address you at the opening of this 16th session of the Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management. We do meet at a strategically important moment for the geospatial community. Here at the UN, we are working to accelerate progress towards the sustainable development goals while looking ahead to sustainable development priorities beyond 2030. And geospatial information, including earth observations, is crucial to both of those. We also see how the pace of the digital transformation is accelerating. Artificial intelligence, advanced analytics and new information sources are shaping how we understand our world, how we design policies, how we adapt to challenges and how we deliver services. Amid such change, trusted and authoritative geospatial information has a crucial role to play. Because development outcomes have geographic locations. Poverty, hunger, disease, environmental degradation, displacement, disasters are human experiences that are rooted in specific communities and places. When decision makers understand not only what is happening, but where it is happening, who is affected, and how conditions differ across places, their interventions can be much more effective. When we talk about the sustainable development goals, we say that we want to leave no one behind, but leaving no one behind may often mean leaving no place behind. And when geospatial information is better integrated with official statistics, administrative data and other sources, its value for granular and timely monitoring makes it uniquely suited to helping define the post 2030 sustainable development agenda. So distinguished delegates. The Committee of Experts has established a clear strategic direction for 2025 to 2030, guided by a vision of geospatial information helping to resolve sustainable development challenges across different geographic scales. The vision is bold and it is timely. So I would like to encourage the committee to continue positioning geospatial information as a foundational component of modern public digital infrastructure, and especially when integrated into the wider data ecosystem as an essential source of evidence and action for sustainable development. Dear colleagues, there does remain a significant divide across countries in the capacities to access and work with geospatial information. So I would also like to commend you for leading global efforts to bridge this geospatial digital divide guided by the committee's frameworks and recommendations. Connecting the committee's normative work with knowledge exchange, with peer learning, with technical assistance and national implementation remains essential. And I commend the regional committees for translating that global guidance into regional and national action and the UN Global Geospatial Centres of Excellence for providing important expertise, innovation and capacity development support. Let me also invite you to engage fully with the wider United Nations system where geospatial expertise is embedded across many policy domains. It could be agriculture, health, climate change, education, urban planning, economic development, marine protection and biodiversity. Together, we need to develop the guidance, the methods, the tools and the knowledge needed to support national geospatial capacity for improving lives. Ladies and gentlemen, later this year, the third United Nations World Geospatial Information Congress will be convened in Jeddah from the 16th to the 19th of November by the United Nations and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. with the theme navigating the next Frontier embracing the digital Renaissance and a new geospatial paradigm the Congress will be an important opportunity to look beyond present systems and to consider how integrated geospatial knowledge information and infrastructure can support a more inclusive resilient and sustainable future I hope to see many of you there and I look forward to your advancing its ambitious agenda. Now, here in New York over the next three days, I look forward to thoughtful and forward-looking deliberations and to practical action. I encourage your wholehearted engagement in these discussions. On our part, DESA stands ready to continue to support the Committee in advancing its work programme, strengthening national capacities and ensuring that geospatial information contributes fully to national priorities, sustainable development and well-being for all. With that, I wish you a very successful 16th session.

Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues. As Bjorn said, it's an honor to open this 16th session of the Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management at the moment where international community is committed into actions of the pact of the future. Two years ago, in September 2024, world leaders adopted the Pact for the Future and its Digital Compact. The Digital Compact is a shared recognition that digital technologies are reshaping every dimension of public life, and also a shared resolve to close that digital divide rather than widen it. And this digital compact calls explicitly for development of a digital public infrastructure grounded on national priorities and needs. And this committee long understood that it needs to execute, implement, and to ensure that Credibility of a digital public infrastructure without geospatial information, it's basically not implementing that digital compact. So the foundational need, role of geospatial information is key. Every service governments deliver somewhere, it has a location, be it a land issue, clinic, flood warnings, broadcast, this location, location, and location. Location is not just a technical add-on into public administration. It's an organizing logic of it. With geospatial information, we need to ensure that, first of all, it's interoperable, it's accessible across entities, and across partners. it becomes what the statistical and connectivity infrastructure already are, foundational national public good. Maybe I should say foundational global public good, once built and reused everywhere, from disaster response to fiscal planning, including to deliver sustainable development goals as Bjorn mentioned in his speech. That's why the work of this committee is not just a technical sideline of the pact of the future. It is the part of how the pact gets implemented. Therefore, through the United Nations Integrated Geospatial Information Framework, jointly with the UN Statistical Commission and the Global Statistical Geospatial Framework, countries should and must benefit from the guidance that this group provides to advance that geospatial information management. Let me tell you about perhaps my dream about what it is that in the future, hopefully in the Congress in Jeddah, the future of GIS includes that as well. In the next decade, geospatial information management should become the real-time digital nervous system of society. I repeat, real-time digital nervous system of society, integrating earth, air, space, cyberspace, even the moon or Mars. The rapid deployment of low orbit satellites, constellations such as Starlink, Amazon, Leo and others is one of the major catalysts for this transformation. And I hope in the next Congress, as well as here, we start also discuss about the future of GIS, which should include satellite trajectories, orbital constellations, debris fields, spectral utilization, space weather, lunar infrastructure to name a few. And these, for those, I mean, a long time in this business, by the way, I'm Mozambican and I started working United Nations back in 1993 in my own country. What got me a job in United Nations to be here today actually was the GIS because I just designed a simple database called D base. I programmed using Clipper, people entered the data, and I used the mapping info to connect the D base with the maps, and I provided the report, and everybody was impressed. And that got me the job that I'm here today. So these transformations represent this shift from 2D to 3D, but also to a 4D and 5D in the future, and GIS is this foundational element there. So I hope that over the coming days, I look forward to hear more from your proceedings on how we need to collectively advance both your frameworks, the standards, and make your special function as an integrated and essential part of digital public infrastructure, reliable, shareable, built to last. And we need to advance that collectively for the people and for the planet. So with that, I wish you a very successful deliberations. And I want to thank all of you for coming all the way from different countries. I understand almost 84 countries taking away times that you would do something else to be here. and to discuss this foundational piece for the path of the future, for the global digital compact, and for humanity, the planet, and for all of us. I thank the Assistant Secretary General and Chief Information Technology Officer of the Office of Information and Communications Technology. The support that he expressed for our work is truly valued and much appreciated. And on behalf of the entire UNGGIM Committee of Experts, I'd like to say thank you and how wonderful it is to be surrounded by leaders who truly understand and get our world. Thank you. Allow me now to say a few words on behalf of the Bureau of the 15th session. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, and friends, as noted by our assistant secretary generals, we meet at a significant moment. The multilateral system is changing before our eyes. Assumptions once considered settled are being questioned. Instructions, institutions are being asked to do more, respond faster and demonstrate their value more clearly. And yet here, countries with different histories, priorities and capacities come together. Not because cooperation is easy, but because the challenges set before us cannot be solved by any country acting alone. Here we demonstrate multilateralism at its most practical. building trust, as we talked about yesterday, agreeing on common principles, and bringing coherence to the global geospatial agenda. This is humanity at its best. Institutions are, in many ways, society's collective memory. They preserve knowledge, establish trust, and provide continuity beyond any one government project or technological cycle. Good governance is therefore not simply about maintaining order. It is about knowing which walls are load bearing, where doors must be open, and where bridges must be built. Geospatial information is one of those bridges. It connects information about our environment, our population, our health, our infrastructure, and the risks confronting our communities. It helps us understand not only what's happening, but where it is happening, who is affected, and where action is most urgently needed. Geospatial information is no longer simply a backdrop to decision making. It is becoming part of the foundation upon which every critical decision is made. But a map is not a policy. A data set does not appropriate a budget. A model does not strengthen a building, protect a coastline, or deploy a rescue system. Turning knowledge into resilience requires more than technology. It requires leadership. Our scientists and technical experts can show us where the risks lie and what the evidence demands. But if that knowledge remains within the technical community, we will have confused insight with impact. We must build a stronger bridge between technical expertise and political decision making, transforming that knowledge into policy, policy into investment, and investment into action. For most of human history, maps have carried us toward the unknown. They help us cross oceans, connect societies, and understand the world beyond the horizon. The history of humanity is on the timeline of exploration, and this is what's next. The next frontier is not an empty space on the map. It is our ability to understand the world as a connected system, to bring together authoritative information, emerging technologies, and human judgment, to govern artificial intelligence responsibly, and to anticipate change before it becomes a crisis. We've never possessed more powerful tools for understanding our planet. But power without governance will not deliver progress. Innovation without inclusion will not deliver equality. And information without action will not secure our future. We cannot settle for isolated islands of resilience in an ocean of vulnerability. Through genuine partnership, We must build resilience across borders, institutions, and communities, ensuring that no person, no place, and no community is left behind. That is the opportunity before the 16th session of the Committee of Experts. Our message is simple, even if the work is not. With the right knowledge, the courage to cooperate, and determination to act, we can meet our national priorities while advancing the common good. Our responsibility now is to turn data into understanding, understanding into decisions, and decisions into a better future. As the Assistant Secretary shared his dream to make geospatial data and all society data the real-time nervous system of our society. Thank you. I thank them once again for joining us today at the opening of our session. Thank you. Thank you so much.

Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Co-Chair, distinguished representatives, delegates, observers and colleagues. It is my privilege to introduce the agenda item Enhancing Geospatial Information Management Arrangement. You have before you a report prepared by the Secretariat with the Bureau for consideration by the Committee of Experts. The Committee of Experts is invited to take note of this comprehensive report and provide its views on activities of the Bureau, the Expanded Bureau and the Secretariat in implementing strategic and practical actions to strengthen and enhance global geospatial information management arrangements with a particular focus on the Sustainable Development Goals and the United Nations Integrated Geospatial Information Framework. The report of the Bureau and the Secretariat provides an overview of the current challenges of the Secretariat, including the reduction of approved geospatial positions dedicated to the Committee and the imminent exhaustion of its extra-budgetary resources supporting the annual committee sessions and proceeding. The report before us highlights the progress made during the intercessional period in advancing the committee's strategic priorities aligned with its strategic framework 2025 to 2030. The priorities identified by the Bureau include the strengthening strategic oversight of the program program agenda and groups, positioning geospatial for sustainable development, updating its main frameworks, chief of which the United Nations integrated geospatial information framework, strengthening the engagement with a wider United Nations system to further anchor geospatial in global agendas, developing a structured multi-year program of work ensuring its primary responsibilities on developing global guidance, encouraging regional implementation, and organizational matters. Over the past year, important efforts have been undertaken to continuously strengthen the committee's institutional architecture, to improve coordination across functional groups, regional committees, thematic networks, and the United Nations Global Geospatial Centres. and reinforce collaboration with the wider United Nations system and international partners. These efforts seek not only to improve governance arrangements, but also to ensure that the Committee's normative work translates into practical implementation, strengthened national capabilities and measurable impact of Member States. I therefore invite delegates to consider the report and consider the points of discussion, including providing guidance on the Committee's strategic priorities for the future programme of work, acknowledge the impact of UN 80 initiative on the secretariat capacity, advise on mobilising extra budgetary resources to support participation by developing countries, encourage participation in the third United Nations geospatial information Congress in November 2026 and provide guidance on preparations for the eighth high level Forum on global geospatial information management in 2028 madam chair I thank you.
